body:
in Archaeology, History, Music |   	November 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

There aren’t many ways to expe­ri­ence the ancient world. We can learn its lan­guages, at least the ones that have left behind deci­pher­able writ­ings; we can behold its arti­facts; we can vis­it its ruins. But noth­ing gets us quite as close to enter­ing the con­scious­ness of our dis­tant fore­bears as hear­ing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archae­ol­o­gist’s Note­book video above, Giselle Kirá­ly gives us a tour through ancient musi­cal his­to­ry, explain­ing the instru­ments of those times that sur­vive in one form or anoth­er today. That tour begins at a much ear­li­er point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punc­tu­at­ing their strug­gle for sur­vival with orga­nized sound.
As evi­dence, Kirá­ly points to the “tiny, exquis­ite­ly craft­ed flutes carved from ani­mal bone and mam­moth ivory” dis­cov­ered on cave floors around Europe. Sur­pris­ing­ly, when played in repli­ca form, these vul­ture- or swan-bone flutes actu­al­ly sound some­what Mid­dle East­ern. But what­ev­er the styl­is­tic traits of the music their orig­i­nal play­ers pro­duced, that music had the poten­tial to con­fer ben­e­fits beyond imme­di­ate plea­sure: “It would’ve con­nect­ed peo­ple, built cohe­sion with­in the com­mu­ni­ty,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the liv­ing with some spir­i­tu­al world.” Each of the oth­er dis­cov­ered or recon­struct­ed instru­ments, like swingable “bull­roar­ers,” bone rasps, and litho­phones (of the kind pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture) would have played its own son­ic part to that end.
Kirá­ly also dis­cuss­es the lav­ish­ly dec­o­rat­ed Lyres of Ur, the world’s old­est sur­viv­ing stringed instru­ments; a 3,500-year-old Egypt­ian long-necked lute with a gui­tar-like fin­ger­board; and a set of 65 Chi­nese bianzhong bells cov­er­ing a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also impor­tant are the means of record­ing it, an ancient exam­ple of which Kirá­ly cites in the Hur­ri­an Hymn to Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the old­est known com­plete musi­cal nota­tion. Cen­turies lat­er, in the Greek-speak­ing world — and in the more mon­u­men­tal form of a mar­ble stele — a man named Seik­i­los record­ed an epi­taph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this old­est com­plete­ly pre­served, ful­ly playable musi­cal com­po­si­tion exhort the lis­ten­er: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients need­ed to hear this no less, per­haps, than we do.
Relat­ed con­tent:
What Did Music in Ancient Rome Sound Like?
What Ancient Greek Music Sound­ed Like: Lis­ten to a Recon­struc­tion That’s “100% Accu­rate”
Hear the Old­est Song in the World: A Sumer­ian Hymn Writ­ten 3,400 Years Ago
2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played Dur­ing Homer’s Time
Hear the World’s Old­est Instru­ment, the “Nean­derthal Flute,” Dat­ing Back Over 43,000 Years
Watch an Archae­ol­o­gist Play the “Litho­phone,” a Pre­his­toric Instru­ment That Let Ancient Musi­cians Play Real Clas­sic Rock
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: 'The Book of the Human Body' Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
description: As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for ou
body:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).
As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.
Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”
Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.
Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History
description: All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of P
body:
All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

	Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

	Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

schema.headline: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History

title: Keira Knightley’s Emerald-Green ‘Atonement’ Gown Heads to Christie’s
description: The stunning emerald-green plunging-back gown worn by actress Keira Knightley in Atonement will be auctioned live in London on December 9 at Christi
body:
The stunning emerald-green plunging-back gown worn by actress Keira Knightley in Atonement will be auctioned live in London on December 9 at Christie’s. It is estimated to fetch between £100,000 and £120,000 ($130,940 to $157,125). In addition, the sale titled Love & Lust: A Literary Guide, will offer a host of items “celebrating the many expressions of love, romance and desire,” per the auction house’s description. This will range from passionate letters and cinematic costumes behind famous romances played out on stage and in literature, including about 30 books, manuscripts, autographed letters and original works dating back centuries.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Knightley wore the silky green ensemble designed by Jacqueline Durran for her role as Cecilia Tallis in the 2007 film Atonement, adapted from Ian McEwan’s acclaimed novel, and directed by Joe Wright. The dress last went under the hammer in a charity auction in 2008 and fetched £35,000 ($46,000).

	Also for sale are rare examples of early film poster art, including one of the influential film Metropolis, made in 1926 for its premiere, estimated at £100,000 to £130,000 ($130,940 to $170,220). Another poster for Dracula (1931), which marked a pivotal moment for early sound movies, is being offered for an estimated £80,000 to £120,000 ($104,750 to $157,125).

	These lots are joined, among others, by early 19th-century love letters from the celebrated British Royal Navy officer Horatio Nelson to Emma, Lady Hamilton, estimated at £5,000 and £8,000, plus original sketches by Chris Foss for the publication of The Joy of Sex (1972), estimated at £6,000 to £8,000.

	“Love and desire have inspired some of the most enduring stories in literature and art, and this sale brings together a wonderfully eclectic group of objects that capture their many facets…” jointly stated Thais Hitchins, associate specialist, and Mark Wiltshire, specialist, Christie’s London.

schema.headline: Keira Knightley’s Emerald-Green ‘Atonement’ Gown Heads to Christie’s

title: Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum
description: A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transf
body:
A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro. 

	While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

	In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

	The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

	“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.
	

	The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

	As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

schema.headline: Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum

title: Rachel Whiteread Has Designed the 2027 Brit Awards Trophy
description: Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The
body:
Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

	The trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

	In designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.

schema.headline: Rachel Whiteread Has Designed the 2027 Brit Awards Trophy

title: German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth
description: We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this mo
body:
We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

	“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

	“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

	One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.
	

	However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.


			
			
			
	
			
					“GYM. Fit with Art” at Kunstpalast, Düsseldorf, Photo: Maris Prieditis.
	



	As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

	“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

	Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

schema.headline: German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth
